name: Lip microneedling

card.summary: Needling aimed at lip lines and volume; established for scars elsewhere but unstudied on lips.
card.note: Infection risk if done in non-medical settings.

quick.overview:
Lip microneedling uses fine needles on the lips to try to smooth lines and add a little fullness.

No lip-specific studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Tiny punctures are thought to trigger skin repair and collagen production.
quick.risks: Infection is the key concern, particularly with unregulated providers; a 2024 CDC report linked HIV cases to a spa microneedling facial.

lead: Lip microneedling applies collagen induction therapy, repeated puncturing of the skin with fine sterile needles, to the lips and the skin around them. People use it to soften vertical lip lines, smooth texture and give the lips a slightly fuller, more even look, working through the skin's repair response and new collagen formation.[1][2]

The best-known study is a 2012 trial in The Journal of Dermatological Treatment by Fabbrocini and colleagues, in which ten women aged 50 to 65 received two collagen induction sessions for upper lip wrinkles. Wrinkle severity was greatly reduced in most participants, and the authors called the technique effective and safe for the purpose.[2]

Microneedling more broadly is used for acne scarring and, in some studies, alongside minoxidil for hair loss, and Wikipedia notes that research is ongoing.[1] Its main reported hazards come from unregulated settings, such as the 2024 CDC report of HIV diagnoses in three women after platelet-rich-plasma microneedling facials at an unlicensed spa.[1]

chain: Fine needles make controlled micro-punctures in lip-area skin
Skin repair is triggered and new collagen forms over weeks
Lip lines look softer and the lip area smoother
angle.text: People microneedle the lips and the skin above them to soften upper-lip lines and refine texture, using the collagen-forming repair response. A small published study in women with upper lip wrinkles reported marked reductions in wrinkle severity after two sessions.

paras: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy or dermarolling, punctures the skin repeatedly with fine needles. It is used for scars and acne, and combinations with platelet-rich plasma have unproven efficacy pending studies.[1] For the lips, it is generally aimed at the vertical lines above the upper lip and at the lip border skin rather than at the red lip itself.[2]

Providers and users describe lip microneedling as a way to soften lines, even out texture and help lips look fuller. The rationale is that micro-injuries prompt the skin to rebuild collagen over the following weeks.[2]

Infection is the main concern. In April 2024 the CDC reported HIV diagnoses in three women who had received platelet-rich-plasma microneedling facials at one unregulated spa, prompting warnings about non-medical settings; about 200 other former clients tested negative.[1] In September 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health had warned that such businesses could spread blood-borne infections.[1]

A 2012 study by Fabbrocini and colleagues treated ten women aged 50 to 65 with two collagen induction sessions for upper lip wrinkles. Wrinkle depth was assessed with digital photographs and computerised analysis of silicone skin impressions, and wrinkle severity was greatly reduced in most patients. The authors concluded the technique was effective and safe for upper lip wrinkles.[2] The sample was small and uncontrolled. Other microneedling studies concern scarring and hair loss.[1]

timeline.event: Fabbrocini et al. publish a study of collagen induction therapy for upper lip wrinkles.[2]
New Mexico Department of Health warns about infection risk from PRP microneedling at an unregulated business.[1]
CDC announces three HIV diagnoses linked to an Albuquerque spa's microneedling facials.[1]
